I added `.github/workflows/lawcheck.yml`, copied from the `lawcheck docs ci` example. I did not run the workflow itself. I did run `lawcheck check --base main` locally, and it passed with exit 0.

The workflow runs on pull requests, merge queues and pushes to `main`. It does a full-history checkout with `persist-credentials: false`, sets up Node 24 and runs `npm install`. It then runs `lawcheck check` against the right base. When the base has a `.lawcheck/law.yaml`, it runs the check a second time with `--law-from` set to the base. That second run catches a pull request that loosens the law.

The project already lists `lawcheck` as a dev dependency and has a `package-lock.json`, so I changed nothing else. The workflow isn't committed.

The local check also noted that the `refund` branch itself changes the law. It adds the `clear-errors` rule and `.lawcheck/config.yaml`, which is why the second check will matter once this is merged.

I didn't add `--strict`. The docs suggest it only once the repository has no existing findings.
